title: Hell in Second Temple Judaism
hook: Did Jesus' hearers mean by Sheol, Hades, Gehenna and Tartarus what we mean by hell?
tldr: Between 516 BC and AD 70, Jewish ideas of the afterlife changed. Sheol became Greek Hades, 1 Enoch gave the dead compartments and an accursed valley, and Tartarus became a prison for fallen angels. Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes disagreed, and later rabbis made Gehenna mostly temporary. The video argues that none of this amounts to one fixed doctrine of eternal torment.
big_idea: Second Temple Jews held many views of punishment, not one hell.

points.title: Greek thought reshaped Jewish views
points.text: The video argues that First Temple Jews had no concept of afterlife punishment. By Jesus' day, Greek influence from Plato, Socrates and mythology had led some Second Temple Jews to see the afterlife as a place of punishment too.

points.title: Gehenna began as a real valley
points.text: In the Hebrew Bible the Valley of Hinnom was where children were burned to Molech. It became a place of slaughter and unburied, shamed bodies, and Jeremiah promised it would one day be holy to the Lord.

points.title: Three schools, three answers
points.text: Pharisees taught rewards and punishments after death. Sadducees denied any afterlife. Essenes, Josephus reports, sent good souls to a blessed region and bad souls to a dark den. There was no consensus.

points.title: 1 Enoch redrew the map
points.text: 1 Enoch 22 divides the dead into hollow places until judgment. Chapter 27 describes an accursed valley near Jerusalem. The video says 1 Enoch is the first place Sheol and Gehenna merge into one place.

points.title: Rabbinic Gehenna was mostly temporary
points.text: Later rabbis taught that sinners spend time in Gehenna, can repent even at its gates, and are punished no more than twelve months. The video notes that some rabbis said three months.

points.title: Tartarus is for fallen angels
points.text: Tartarus comes from Greek myth, where Zeus imprisoned the Titans. 2 Peter 2:4 uses it only for angels held for judgment, echoing 1 Enoch, where Uriel is over Tartarus. It never describes people.

points.title: Three views, starting with infernalism
points.text: The video introduces three orthodox views of hell. It begins with infernalism, or eternal conscious torment, and questions it with verses, the history of language, and the behaviour of those who claim to believe it.

sections.summary: The video repeats that a view of hell is not a salvation issue. God loves those who believe in eternal torment and those who do not. No view is an absolute certainty, only a possibility, so it gives information and lets viewers decide. It mourns friendships of thirty years broken over differing views of hell.

Jesus was in the grave three days and preached to the captives, yet when he returned no disciple asked him where he had been. They asked about the kingdom instead. In the 18 sermons in Acts, hell never comes up, and Paul never mentions hell to the Gentile churches. The video suggests the hell Jesus warned of happened in the first century.

To Old Testament Jews, Gehenna meant something very different. By Jesus' day, some beliefs had changed and the afterlife was also seen as a place of punishment. The video attributes this to Greek influence from Plato, Socrates and Greek mythology. So the Second Temple Jews Jesus spoke to differed from First Temple Jews.

The Valley of Hinnom was known as an evil place. 2 Chronicles 28:3 says King Ahaz burned his sons in fire there, a practice of the nations the Lord drove out. 2 Kings 23:10 says Josiah defiled Topheth so no one could burn a son or daughter to Molech. Afterwards it remained a site for burning pagan artifacts.

In Jeremiah 7:31, God says burning sons and daughters in the fire was something he did not command, nor did it come into his mind. The video notes that burning people was an abomination under the old covenant. So why think God will do it to most of humanity forever? Jeremiah then renames Hinnom the Valley of Slaughter.

sections.h: A valley of shame for the unburied
sections.summary: The video says criminals, murderers, thieves and lepers were judged and dumped there. Being left unburied, eaten by worms and burned was great shame, and it affected whether one was atoned for after death. Isaiah 66:24 pictures such corpses. Jesus' own body might have gone there had Joseph not buried him.

Readers must decide whether these prophecies were fulfilled when Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 587 BC, or in AD 66-70 when Rome destroyed it. The video holds that AD 70 fulfilled Jesus' words in Matthew 23-24. 'The last days' meant the last days of the old covenant, the temple and its sacrifices, not the end of time.

Jeremiah 31:38-40 says the whole valley of dead bodies and ashes will be holy to the Lord and never torn down again. The same chapter promises a new covenant, with the law written on hearts. Ezekiel 47 has waters flowing from the temple to the Dead Sea, bringing life. A place made holy, the video argues, is no eternal torment.

The video names three main schools. Pharisees believed the soul survives death and receives rewards or punishments. Sadducees denied the soul's afterlife and any punishment: you slept with your fathers, and the soul that sins dies. Essenes held that good souls dwell on a blessed island while the wicked are tormented in a dungeon.

The video says the first place Sheol and Gehenna merge into one place is 1 Enoch. Its Book of Similitudes (Parables) describes the punishment of sinners in more detail than any other Jewish writing. Punishment in Isaiah and Daniel came late and was a minority view. With no consensus, the video says no one should be dogmatic.

Citing Ariela Pelaia's article 'What Is Gehenna?', the video notes Gehenna is not in the Torah and appears in no Jewish text before the sixth century BC. Some rabbinic texts say God created it on the second day of creation (Genesis Rabbah 4:6, 11:9). Others say it was created before the earth. The idea likely grew from Sheol.

sections.h: Rabbinic Gehenna: who, how, how long
sections.summary: Rabbis taught that those who did not follow God's law would spend some time in Gehenna. Idolatry, incest, adultery, pride, anger, losing one's temper and speaking ill of a scholar merited it. Good deeds, Torah, humility and fear of heaven saved one (Midrash on Proverbs 17:1). One could repent at its very gates. Most rabbis set twelve months; some, says the video, three.

sections.h: Jesus knew what they had been taught
sections.summary: Jesus knew this was what his hearers had been taught. So when he said Gehenna, he knew what would be in their minds: a place of limited stay, not an eternal torture chamber. The video says his warning pointed mainly to AD 70 and those who rejected his message. Whether it also has afterlife implications, it says, it does not know.

The Greek tartaroo means to imprison or enchain; being thrown in was to be 'tartarized'. It is a participle, not a noun, rendered hell. In Greek myth it is the deepest part of Hades, where Zeus sent monsters and Titans, named in Hesiod's Theogony about 700 years before Christ. The video calls it the only one of the four words with eternal torment built in.

Even using Greek mythology, 2 Peter 2:4 is about where God sent fallen angels, not people; Jude 1:6 alludes to it. The video says pagan legislators used the idea to control unruly mobs while educated pagans ridiculed it. It adds that Martin Luther wanted 2 Peter, Jude, James and Revelation out of the canon.

Paul seemed to have no definitive view of hell. He never used Gehenna and focused on the gospel's redemptive side. He mentioned Hades only to celebrate its powerlessness and Christ's victory over death. He spoke of judgment generally and used eternal for the saved, but never specified the fate of the wicked. The original hearers would not have thought of eternal torment.

The video introduces three major views of hell that are orthodox, not heresy, though by the 1800s people called each other heretics. Infernalism, or eternal conscious torment (ECT), is the traditional Western view: perhaps most people are not saved, each is judged once at death, and hell is endless conscious punishment with no exit. The video asks whether that makes the cross a failure.

Some take the torment literally, others as spiritual suffering or separation from God. Some grade punishment by sin. Calvinists stress God's sovereign choice, others human freedom; Catholics add purgatory. The video calls it retributive justice that even Moses would not have taught. Cited verses include Daniel 12:1-2, Matthew 18:6-9, Matthew 25:31-46, Mark 9:42-48, Jude 12-13 and Revelation 14 and 20.

sections.h: Latin, the fathers and a thought to ponder
sections.summary: The video says eternal torment became dominant only after Latin replaced Greek as the common language and scholars used the Latin Vulgate, finished in the early 400s. Early Greek fathers did not seem to support it as a whole. It names Tertullian, Augustine, Clement of Rome, Justin Martyr, Hippolytus and Cyprian as infernalists, and asks why believers are not warning everyone constantly.

When the Hebrew Scriptures were translated into Greek in Alexandria around 200 BC, the Septuagint used Hades for Sheol, because of its likeness to the Greek underworld. The match is approximate. Sheol had no clear two-part division, but Greek Hades did, and some early Jewish works separated the righteous dead from the unrighteous by a river or chasm.

In 1 Enoch 22, from the Book of the Watchers, Enoch sees hollow places in a western mountain where the spirits of the dead wait for the day of judgment. Raphael explains the divisions. The righteous have a bright spring of water. Sinners who escaped judgment in life suffer pain there, and a place is kept for those unjustly killed, like Abel.

sections.h: Research: the accursed valley of 1 Enoch 27
sections.summary: In 1 Enoch 27, Enoch asks why an accursed valley lies in the blessed land, and Uriel says it is for those cursed forever. Bart Ehrman calls this the earliest evidence outside the Hebrew Bible for Gehenna as divine punishment, and the Jewish Encyclopedia identifies it with Hinnom. Chaim Milikowsky cautions that the text never names Gehenna.

In 1 Enoch 20:2, the archangel Uriel is set over Tartarus, and other chapters bind the fallen Watchers in darkness until the judgment. Commentators see this as the background of 2 Peter 2:4, which uses the verb tartaroo, and of Jude 6. Both letters speak of angels kept for a coming judgment, not of humans.

Josephus (Jewish War 2.155) says the Essenes sent good souls to a calm region beyond the ocean, and bad souls to 'a dark and tempestuous den, full of never-ceasing punishments'. He compares this to the Greeks' Isles of the Blessed. This matches the video's point that Greek ideas shaped how some Jews pictured the afterlife.

The Dead Sea Scrolls' Community Rule curses the wicked to 'the gloom of everlasting fire'. It also speaks of eternal destruction and 'shameful extinction in the fire of the dark regions', with no remnant or survivor. Conditionalists read this as punishment ending in total destruction, others as endless torment. Even this one community's text is debated.

The Talmud (Eruvin 19a) teaches that even at the gates of Gehinnom a person can repent. The Jewish Encyclopedia notes that later Judaism saw Gehenna as a kind of purgatory for faithless Jews and as perdition for Gentiles. Pesahim 54a counts it among things created before the world. Most rabbinic sources treat it as a temporary, purifying stay.

mythfact.myth: Jews always believed in punishment after death.
mythfact.fact: The video argues that early Jewish tradition focused on burial, shame and atonement. Afterlife punishment emerged later in Second Temple Judaism, shaped partly by Greek thought.

mythfact.myth: Gehenna was always a name for an eternal hell.
mythfact.fact: In the Hebrew Bible it is a real valley of sacrifice and slaughter, promised to become holy. Later rabbis mostly limited its punishment to twelve months.

mythfact.myth: Tartarus in 2 Peter is where sinful humans go.
mythfact.fact: 2 Peter 2:4 echoes 1 Enoch's fallen Watchers. It describes angels held for judgment, never human beings.

mythfact.myth: Sheol and Hades are exactly the same thing.
mythfact.fact: The Septuagint used Hades for Sheol, but the match is approximate. Greek Hades had divisions that Hebrew Sheol lacked, which later Jewish texts adopted.

terms.meaning: Jewish religion from the rebuilt Temple in 516 BC to its destruction by Rome in AD 70.

The traditional Western view, also called eternal conscious torment (ECT): endless punishment with no exit.

quiz.q: According to the video, which Jewish group denied the soul's afterlife and any punishment?
quiz.why: The Sadducees held that you simply slept with your fathers. Acts 23:8 also says they denied resurrection and spirits.

quiz.q: In 1 Enoch 20:2, which angel is set over Tartarus?
quiz.why: 1 Enoch names Uriel over the world and Tartarus. 2 Peter 2:4 echoes this tradition of fallen angels imprisoned until judgment.

quiz.q: What did the Septuagint use to translate Sheol?
quiz.why: Greek-speaking Jewish translators used Hades, the Greek underworld, for Sheol. Its divisions later shaped Jewish pictures of the dead.

reflect: If Jesus' hearers held many views of the afterlife, which one did his Gehenna warnings actually assume?

objections.claim: Most Second Temple literature taught endless torment, so Jesus' hearers would have heard Gehenna as eternal conscious torment.
objections.strongest: Defenders of eternal torment argue that the preponderance of Apocrypha, Pseudepigrapha, Qumran and rabbinic texts portray the wicked's torment as endless. 1 Enoch 27 reserves the accursed valley for those cursed forever. Jesus used Gehenna without correcting this.
objections.response: The evidence is real but mixed. 1 Enoch 22 describes a holding place until judgment. Scholars like Chaim Milikowsky note that chapter 27 never names Gehenna. The Qumran Community Rule speaks of everlasting fire, yet also of extinction with no survivor. Sadducees denied any afterlife, and later rabbis limited Gehenna to twelve months for most. The video adds that Jesus knew his hearers' rabbinic teaching. Such diversity cannot establish one default meaning.

objections.claim: 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6 show a real underworld prison exists now, so hell as torment is apostolic teaching.
objections.strongest: Peter chose the word Tartarus, which Greeks linked with the worst punishment, and Jude speaks of everlasting chains. If God imprisons angels in darkness, the same justice would apply to the wicked among humans.
objections.response: Both letters draw on 1 Enoch, where the fallen Watchers are bound in darkness and Uriel is set over Tartarus. In each case the prisoners are angels, and they are held for a coming judgment, a custody that implies something beyond itself. Neither text puts a human being in Tartarus. Peter's next examples, the flood and Sodom, involve humans destroyed, not tormented. Borrowing a cultural image to make a point does not endorse Greek mythology about the dead.

objections.claim: Sheol always had two compartments, so the wicked suffer conscious torment immediately at death, as Luke 16 shows.
objections.strongest: Many traditional teachers hold that Sheol or Hades had a blessed side, Abraham's bosom, and a side of torment. 1 Enoch 22 confirms that Jews of Jesus' day divided the dead, and Luke 16 puts the rich man in torment at once.
objections.response: 1 Enoch 22 does divide the dead, but this is a Second Temple development, not the Hebrew Bible's picture. Old Testament Sheol had no clearly defined two-part division. The divided Hades came in through Greek translation and Hellenistic Jewish writings, which is exactly the Greek influence the video describes. Even in Enoch, the hollow places are temporary, holding souls until the day of judgment. So they cannot by themselves prove endless torment.

objections.claim: The video's history is loose: the death toll, the bodies in Gehenna and Luther's canon do not all check out.
objections.strongest: Josephus gives about 1.1 million deaths in the siege, a figure many think inflated, and does not say they were thrown into Hinnom. Luther set apart Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation, not 2 Peter. Such errors weaken the argument.
objections.response: These corrections are fair and should be granted. The video's figure of 1.2 to 1.3 million exceeds Josephus' 1.1 million, and the claim that bodies were dumped in Hinnom goes beyond his text. Luther's 1522 New Testament separated Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation. Yet the central claims stand on other evidence: the Hebrew Bible's valley of slaughter, the Sadducee and Essene disagreements in Josephus, 1 Enoch's Watchers behind 2 Peter, and rabbinic limits on Gehenna.
